Comparing Cloud Providers

This content was generated with the assistance of AI and should be verified against the official documentation before being relied on in production.

See the bibliographies of the Azure, AWS and Google Cloud sections for the reference material consulted while preparing these pages.

This page compares the three public cloud providers documented in this section, AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, on popularity, ecosystem, learning curve, pricing, availability regions and a few other metrics. It ends with a recommendation by workload type and target region, plus a decision flowchart. All figures are a snapshot as of 2026-10-26: each number is linked to a source listed in the Bibliography, and the data files behind the tables and figures are kept in the repository under scripts/cloud-comparison-charts/data.

The scope is deliberately limited to the three providers above. Other providers, such as Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Alibaba Cloud and IBM Cloud, exist and matter in some markets, but they are mentioned for context only and are not scored. The Gartner positioning in Analyst positioning notes, for example, that Alibaba Cloud was also named a Leader in 2026.

Methodology

Sources, dates and missing data

Every row of every data file has a source id and a retrieval date (2026-10-26, the snapshot date). Primary and official sources are preferred: the providers' earnings releases, official pricing pages and price-list files, official region and service-availability pages, SLA documents, and recognised analyst and survey publications. Source ids appear next to each table or figure as links into the Bibliography, which lists every source with its publication or access date. Blogs and unsourced aggregators are not used for numbers.

A value for which no reliable public source was found is shown as n/a (not available). It is never plotted as zero and never estimated. Where a figure had to come from a secondary source because the primary page could not be read, it is labelled as secondary in the text:

  • JetBrains State of Developer Ecosystem 2025 is taken from an AWS Insider report, because the JetBrains page returned an access error.

  • Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026 usage, admired and desired figures are taken from a Virtualization Review article dated 2026-10-06, because the survey page text had no per-provider figures.

  • Canalys (Omdia) quarterly shares come from search-engine excerpts of the publisher pages, which returned an access error when fetched, so some provider shares are missing.

  • Gartner Magic Quadrant positioning for 2020 to 2022 comes from press coverage, and the 2025 and 2026 positioning of AWS and Google Cloud comes from the providers' own statements. The Gartner reports themselves are not public.

Caveats that apply to the whole page

  • Synergy Research Group and Canalys (Omdia) market-share series are different series with different scopes and methods and must not be spliced together.

  • Synergy changed its treatment of Microsoft from the third quarter of 2024: some Azure revenue was reclassified as software as a service, which lowered Microsoft’s share from that release onward. The share series has a break at that point.

  • Revenue segments are not like for like: AWS reports segment net sales, Google Cloud reports a segment that includes Google Workspace, Microsoft reports Intelligent Cloud, which is broader than Azure, and discloses Azure only as a growth rate.

  • Developer surveys measure different populations and wordings, so their percentages are not comparable across surveys.

  • A region or an availability zone is not defined identically by the three providers, and the Azure count used here is the number of regions listed on the Microsoft regions page, which may include regions that are not open to every customer.

  • Prices are list prices on the retrieval date, on demand, in US dollars, without taxes, discounts, free allowances or support plans. They are not a quote.

Criteria and score derivation

The radar chart in Scorecard uses six axes scored from 0 to 10, where 10 means best of the three providers on that axis (not a theoretical maximum). Four axes are computed from the data files by a script, and two are editorial. The rule for each axis is:

Axis Kind Rule

Popularity

Computed

10 times the mean of (Synergy 2026-Q2 share divided by the largest share) and (Stack Overflow 2026 usage divided by the largest usage)

Ecosystem breadth

Computed

10 times the mean of (service categories with a service, out of the 31 mapped) and (official SDK languages divided by the largest count)

Ease of use

Editorial

Judgement from trial credit and length, Stack Overflow admired score, size of the first-party learning catalogue and certification path size

Price competitiveness

Computed

10 times the mean over the four reference architectures of (cheapest monthly list-price total divided by own total)

Regional coverage

Computed

10 times the mean of (generally available public regions divided by the most), (their availability zones divided by the most) and (sovereign categories available out of China, government and sovereign, divided by 3). Region and zone counts come from the footprint data on the same basis for all three providers: China, government and sovereign partitions are left out of the counts, because they are scored by the third term

AI offering

Editorial, low confidence

Judgement from managed ML platform, foundation-model platform, prebuilt AI services and AI certifications; no model-quality or market data was fetched

The scores, the evidence behind each one and the computed-versus-editorial split are given in Scorecard. The data files and their refresh procedure are documented in the repository (scripts/cloud-comparison-charts/data/NOTES.md), and the figures are regenerated from them with npm run charts:cloud-comparison.

Snapshot date and where to check current values

All values are stated as of 2026-10-26 unless a table says otherwise. Cloud pricing, regions and service availability change continuously, so check the live official pages before making a decision:

Metric Where to check current values

Regions and zones

AWS Global Infrastructure; Google Cloud locations; Azure products by region

Per-region services and AI models

AWS Regional Services List; Azure products available by region; Vertex AI locations

Pricing

Azure Retail Prices API; Google Cloud compute pricing; AWS price-list files such as the Amazon EC2 price list

Free tiers

AWS Free Tier; Azure free account; Google Cloud Free Program

Market share

The latest quarterly press releases of Synergy Research Group and Omdia (Canalys), listed in the Bibliography

Revenue

The latest earnings releases of Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft, listed in the Bibliography

Service-level agreements

AWS; Microsoft; Google Cloud

Popularity

Market share

Synergy Research Group publishes a quarterly estimate of worldwide spending on cloud infrastructure services (IaaS, PaaS and hosted private cloud) and each provider’s share of it. In the second quarter of 2026 the total was about USD 143.4 billion, with AWS at 28%, Microsoft at 20% and Google Cloud at 15%. Synergy reports Microsoft as a whole (Azure and related infrastructure and platform services), not Azure alone.

Integration strengths

The sources used measure breadth and tooling, not integration quality, so the strengths below are limited to what they show. Claims about, for example, Microsoft 365 or .NET integration are not quantified by any dataset here and are not scored.

  • AWS: the widest mapped catalogue (31 of 31 categories), the most official SDK languages (11), the most downloaded Terraform provider (about 8.1 billion cumulative downloads against 2.1 billion for Azure and 2.7 billion for Google Cloud), and AWS Ground Station, for which Microsoft states that Azure has no managed equivalent and which the Google comparison page does not list. Sources: svc-ms-aws-index, sdkref-aws, terraform-registry.

  • Azure: Microsoft Entra ID is the mapped identity service, Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions are the mapped CI/CD services, and Azure Arc and Azure Local cover hybrid and edge, a category for which the Google comparison page lists no equivalent. Sources: svc-ms-aws-index, svc-ms-compute.

  • Google Cloud: BigQuery is the mapped data warehouse, Google Kubernetes Engine the mapped managed Kubernetes service, and Infrastructure Manager (Terraform-based) and Config Connector the native infrastructure as code. Sources: svc-gcp-comparison, svc-gcp-infra-manager.

The provider guides on this site cover each ecosystem in depth. Landing pages: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. Compute decision guides: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.

The AWS certification count is a lower bound because the professional tier rendered only partly, and Azure counts role-based and specialty titles containing the word Azure, excluding three marked Legacy. Two of the criteria in the list above, console and IAM complexity and the time to a first reference deployment, have no objective public measurement, and none was invented. The best way to judge them is to follow each provider’s getting-started guide on this site, which walks through a hands-on first deployment: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. The identity pages (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) show how much IAM surface each provider asks a new team to learn.

Provider Strengths shown by the data Pain points shown by the data

AWS

Highest Stack Overflow usage (41.8%), admired (45.8%) and desired (24.1%) scores; a six-month free plan with up to USD 200 of credit; the most community Q&A volume implied by its usage

The widest service surface (31 mapped categories) means the most to learn; only 11 certifications counted (lower bound); no public learning-catalogue size

Azure

The largest first-party learning catalogue found (283 learning paths and 1,161 modules on Microsoft Learn); 20 Azure certifications, 5 of them AI-named; more than 65 always-free services

The shortest trial window (USD 200 over 30 days); admired score 43.2% is below AWS

Google Cloud

The longest and largest trial (USD 300 over 90 days); the leanest certification set (13), which keeps the learning path short

The lowest admired score of the three (42.6%) and the fewest AI-named certifications (2); no public learning-content counts, so its catalogue could not be compared

The editorial ease-of-use scores that follow from this evidence are 7 for AWS, 7 for Azure and 6.5 for Google Cloud on the 0 to 10 scale. The differences are small, and the score is a judgement, not a measurement.

  • The SKUs compared are listed in the next table. The VM is the closest general-purpose 2 vCPU, 8 GiB shape on each provider, not the same hardware.

  • The PostgreSQL rows are not strictly equivalent: Google Cloud SQL has no burstable 2 vCPU shape, so its price is for a dedicated-core instance (2 vCPU, 4 GiB), against burstable instances on AWS and Azure.

Worked example: four reference architectures

To make the building blocks concrete, one reference architecture per workload type is priced with the same sizing on each provider, in US East, for 730 hours (one month). The totals are computed arithmetically from the list prices in the previous section, with no free allowances, discounts, taxes or support, so each is an upper bound for a small account and not a quote. Totals are the sum of the unrounded line amounts, so a total can differ by one cent from the sum of the rounded lines shown. The inputs are listed in full so that anyone can reproduce them.

The official pricing calculators were not run to produce these totals. They are interactive and cannot be scripted, so the figures here are a hand calculation (quantity times unit price, summed). Mainland China is a separate market with its own legal and operating model, and the three providers differ sharply there:

  • Accounts: an AWS (China) account reaches only the Beijing and Ningxia regions, and accounts are not shared with the global partition. Azure operated by 21Vianet is a physically separated instance run under a separate agreement (OSPA). Google Cloud has no mainland China offering, so a customer there cannot be served from a Google Cloud region in the country.

  • ICP licensing: a public website served from mainland China needs an Internet Content Provider (ICP) filing with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) if it is non-commercial, or a value-added telecommunications licence (the ICP licence) if it is commercial, on either provider. The customer obtains it and pays any government fees; the operators help with the paperwork. AWS says Sinnet (Beijing) and NWCD (Ningxia) support ICP requests at no extra charge, and that you may have to show the filing or licence before you host public content. On Amazon S3 in the China regions, anonymous GET requests and pre-signed URLs work only when the account has a valid ICP licence, so a public S3 static website needs one too. Microsoft says a domain without an ICP filing is not allowed online, and the filed domain must resolve to a filed IP address. A public security (PSB) filing is also due within 30 days of launch, or 21Vianet may suspend access. Both providers also require a legal entity in China (Azure) or a separate China account (AWS), so plan the filing before the launch date. Google Cloud has no mainland China region, so it has no ICP path of its own.

  • Service parity: Microsoft describes a feature parity gap with global Azure that is narrowing. No parity measurement was found for AWS China, so none is given.

  • Latency: the nearest Google Cloud regions to mainland China are Hong Kong (asia-east2) and Taiwan (asia-east1), as derived from the list of 43 regions. No latency measurements were gathered for this page.

Minimum monthly price of the entry, production and enterprise tiers. Plans are not like for like. AWS Business Support Plus is the greater of USD 29 or 9% of the first USD 10,000 of monthly charges, and AWS lists no separate production tier on the page fetched. Azure plans are flat monthly prices (Developer, Standard and Professional Direct), and Microsoft does not publish a price for Unified Enterprise. Google Cloud plans are the greater of a minimum or a percentage of charges (Standard 3%, Enhanced 10% down to 3% in tiers, Premium from USD 15,000). AWS Enterprise Support is 10% of the first USD 150,000 down to 3% in tiers. Sources: aws-support, azure-support, gcp-support.

Reliability and incident history

No reliable like-for-like incident history was found, so none is compared. AWS publishes no public machine-readable incident history for the window. The Azure post-incident review list is rendered by script, and the fetched view covered only two reports from 2026-09-29 and 2026-09-30. Google Cloud’s incident feed held only 8 incidents between February and October 2026, not a full 12 months. A count of incidents from such partial data would be misleading. Sources: aws-health, azure-status-history, gcp-status.

Summary: which provider to choose

The recommendation below is drawn only from the metrics in the previous sections. Each cell is the fit of a provider for a workload (best fit, good fit or acceptable) with a relative index in brackets, where the best provider on the metric is 100. Fit is best at an index of 95 or more, good from 80 and acceptable below. The matrix is computed from the data files, so it matches the figure and can be regenerated.

The first four rows are the workload types, priced by the reference architectures. The next four are cross-cutting needs and are scored from the radar axes. The static website, dynamic site and microservices rows use list-price totals only, and the AI row averages the price index with the share of model and region combinations available (17 of 18 for AWS, 12 of 18 for Azure and for Google Cloud). The index for ease of use is based on an editorial score, and the index for hiring and community support on the popularity score, which includes survey usage (a secondary source for 2026). The optional data analytics and warehousing and batch and high-performance computing workload types are not rated, because no metric for them was gathered. The service mapping only shows that BigQuery, Azure Synapse Analytics and Amazon Redshift are the mapped data warehouses. Enterprise and Microsoft-centric workloads are rated qualitatively below, from the evidence already on this page.

Enterprise and Microsoft-centric workloads (editorial)

This row is not part of the computed matrix and has no index. It is an editorial reading of two sourced facts from earlier sections, and integration quality itself (Microsoft 365, .NET tooling) is still not measured:

  • Licence cost: Azure Hybrid Benefit is the only licence-reuse discount in the discount data, at up to 80% for Windows Server VMs and up to 85% for SQL Server (see Discount models). The discount data has no equivalent entry for AWS or Google Cloud, so Azure is the only one of the three for which this page quantifies a saving when existing Windows Server and SQL Server licences with Software Assurance are moved to the cloud.

  • Identity: Microsoft Entra ID is Azure’s mapped identity service (see Integration strengths), so an organisation that already runs Entra ID for Microsoft 365 starts with its identity provider in place.

Workload AWS Azure Google Cloud Basis

Enterprise and Microsoft-centric

acceptable

best

acceptable

Editorial, from the Hybrid Benefit discount data and the Entra ID service mapping; no index

The rating says only that Azure has a documented licence and identity advantage for these workloads. AWS and Google Cloud both run Windows Server and SQL Server and offer their own licensing options, which this comparison did not gather, so check them before deciding on cost alone.

What the metrics say, workload by workload

  • Static website: Azure and AWS are best fit and within 4 percent on list price (USD 46.59 and 48.20 per month for the reference site), while Google Cloud is acceptable at USD 63.05, mainly because of its egress price. How-to guides: AWS static hosting, Azure Blob Storage and Google Cloud static sites.

  • Simple dynamic site: Azure (USD 144.95) and AWS (USD 147.08) are best fit. Google Cloud (USD 186.13) is acceptable, partly because its PostgreSQL shape is a dedicated-core instance. Compute guides: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.

  • Microservices: Azure (USD 435.54) and AWS (USD 447.30) are best fit, Google Cloud (USD 507.43) is a good fit. All three charge the same USD 0.10 per hour for the managed Kubernetes control plane. Guides: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.

  • Services using AI: the LLM price is identical on all three, so cost does not separate them (USD 991.06 on Azure, 995.48 on AWS and 1,002.00 on Google Cloud). Availability does: AWS offers the checked models in 17 of 18 combinations, against 12 of 18 for Azure and Google Cloud, so AWS is best fit and the other two are good fit. The result is specific to the models and regions checked. The AI offering radar score (editorial, low confidence) rates Azure highest. AI guides: AWS, Azure (with Foundry Tools) and Google Cloud.

The flowchart is a starting point and is limited to the data in this page. Re-run the comparison with current prices and the services, models and regions you actually need before committing.
